title: Histogram and ECDF: what is the distribution?
summary: What does a set of measurements look like? A histogram shows the shape of a large sample and the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) shows a small sample without binning. Together they answer where the values lie, how spread they are and whether the shape is symmetric.

media.alt: Two panels: left, a teal histogram of 200 values with density on the y axis, ten bars from about 0.4 to 4.5 peaking near 2.1 and an amber dashed median line at 2.41; right, an ECDF staircase of 25 points rising from 0 to 1 with a dotted blue normal-fit curve to its lower right and a horizontal amber line at 0.5.
media.caption: Reference render of class F8.1 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What is the distribution?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: value (unit) on x, density on y; the bin rule is written under the x label. Right: value (unit) on x, cumulative fraction (0 to 1) on y; the ECDF is a step function with a dot at each observation.
look_at: Where is the bulk of the data, and is the shape symmetric, skewed or does it have a shoulder or two humps?
Is the bin rule stated and does a different bin width change the story?
On the ECDF, where does the curve cross 0.5 (the median), and how steep is it (where the data are concentrated)?
How does the ECDF compare with a reference curve, and is the sample behind each panel stated?
as_drawn: Left: n = 200 values, 10 bins of width 0.46 by the Freedman-Diaconis rule (written under the axis), density scale, median line at 2.41. The shape has a peak near 2.1 and a long right shoulder out to 4.5.
Right: an ECDF of only the first 25 values with a dot at each step, a normal curve fitted to all 200 values (dotted blue) and a median line at 0.5. The ECDF crosses 0.5 near 2.0, not 2.4.
The ECDF subsample is not a random subsample: it is the first 25 draws, all from the lower group, so it sits left of the fitted normal; this is a feature of the demonstration, not evidence of misfit.
No uncertainty band is drawn on the ECDF; with 25 points a 95 percent band is plus or minus 0.27.
read_the_figure.proves: The histogram shows the shape of the sample; the ECDF shows exactly which fraction lies below any value, with no binning choice. Neither proves what distribution generated the data.
if_wrong: A histogram with a different bin width telling a different story: the shape depends on a choice that has to be stated.
ECDF compared with a reference curve fitted to a different sample: the gap is not evidence of misfit.
A normal curve drawn through skewed data: the median and the mean do not coincide.
must_check: bin rule stated: the shape of a histogram depends on the bin width, so the rule that set it must be written on the figure.
ECDF for small n: with few points a histogram is mostly empty bins and noise, while the ECDF uses every observation.

terms.meaning: Counts (or density) of observations in adjacent bins, drawn as bars.
Bar area, not height, equals the fraction of data in the bin, so that the total area is 1.
A bin width of twice the inter-quartile range times n to the power -1/3.
The fraction of observations less than or equal to x; a staircase that rises by 1/n at each observation.
The value below which half the observations lie, where the ECDF crosses 0.5.
A confidence band for the whole ECDF of half-width sqrt(ln(2/alpha) / (2n)).

remember: Bin width by Freedman-Diaconis: w = 2 IQR n^(-1/3).
Density bars: area = fraction, so height = fraction / width.
ECDF: F_n(x) = (number of values at most x) / n.
DKW: for n = 25 the 95 percent band is plus or minus 0.27; for n = 200 it is 0.096.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: In the histogram, the horizontal position of a bar marks a range of values and its height the density, so area is probability; the amber dashed line marks the median. In the ECDF, position on x is the value and height on y the cumulative fraction; each dot is one observation and the staircase joins them. The dotted blue line is a reference model, and the horizontal amber line marks 0.5.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: before you model data, look at it. A histogram piles values into bins so the eye sees where they cluster. For a handful of values, bins are mostly empty and the picture depends on where the edges fall; the ECDF avoids this by drawing every point. Reading it is easy: the height at x is the fraction of data below x, so steep parts are where the data are dense and flat parts where there are gaps.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Bin width changes the picture: too wide hides a second hump, too narrow makes noise look like structure. A density axis makes the heights depend on the unit of the data. The ECDF is hard to read for shape and for skew without practice. A reference curve fitted to a different sample than the ECDF (as here) makes any difference look like misfit. And neither shows uncertainty unless a band is added.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A kernel density estimate gives a smooth curve (with its own bandwidth choice). A box plot or a violin plot compares many groups compactly. A QQ plot (F8.7) is the sharper tool for comparing with a normal distribution. A rug of the raw points under the histogram shows the data.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Draw the 95 percent DKW band around the ECDF, plot the ECDF of the full sample on the same axes as the normal fit, add a rug under the histogram, and show two bin widths side by side.

steps.title: The bin rule
steps.note: The Freedman-Diaconis width for the render's data; Sturges' rule would give 9 bins.

steps.title: The empirical distribution function
steps.note: A step of 1/n at each observation; the median is where F_n reaches 0.5.

steps.title: How uncertain is an ECDF?
steps.note: The Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality gives a band that holds for the whole curve at once.

worked.title: Reading the histogram and the ECDF of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What fraction of the 200 values lies in the tallest bar? (2) From the ECDF, what fraction of the 25 values lies between 1 and 2? (3) How uncertain is that ECDF?

solution.text: (1) The tallest bar has a density of about 0.45 and a width of 0.46.
(2) The ECDF is about 0.20 at x = 1 and about 0.50 at x = 2.
(3) With 25 points the DKW half-width at 95 percent is 0.27, so every height on the curve could be off by that much.

worked.answer: About 21 percent of the values (about 42) are in the tallest bar; about 30 percent of the subsample lies between 1 and 2; the ECDF is uncertain by plus or minus 0.27 everywhere.

checks.q: Why is an ECDF better than a histogram for 25 values?
checks.answer: A histogram of 25 values has mostly empty or one-count bins that depend on the bin edges; the ECDF uses every value and has no binning choice.

checks.q: n = 100, IQR = 2. What is the Freedman-Diaconis bin width?
An ECDF is steep between 1.9 and 2.1 and flat between 2.1 and 2.9. What does that say about the data?
checks.answer: Many values cluster between 1.9 and 2.1 and there are none between 2.1 and 2.9: a peak followed by a gap (a possible second group beyond it).
